highlights.text: a single underlying sense — withering and scarcity of water/moisture — runs through both the non-hamzated and hamzated forms of this root
Hamzated form, al-ẓamaʾ: thirst.
a single root whose core sense is the extension or spreading-out of a thing
al-basṭa in anything means amplitude or ample scope
He cites a verse describing "a wide expanse [basāṭ] for the feet of swift she-camels"
one well-known root whose core meaning is pushing a thing aside or removing it
Basic sense — to push, repel, drive away
Shāhid from Ḥumayd: "And they brought forward for departure every prized camel."
دَلَوْتُ الدَّلْوَ means to send the bucket down into the well
Form V, التَّدَلِّي: drawing near, and letting oneself down or hanging low
cast your bucket in among the buckets
One core meaning: pushing/thrusting.
al-disār — the palm-fiber cord binding a ship's planks together (plural dusur)
a line of poetry about a warrior formidable enough to uproot a mountain with a single thrust
a single sound root whose core idea is clinging to and staying fastened
غَرَام (gharām) — punishment that clings
the pre-Islamic poet al-Aʿshā: if such a one punishes, the punishment is inescapable
derives two distinct senses from the root h-y-j
hāja al-baql — said of herbage turning yellow just before it dries out.
by the poet Ru'ba: he describes finding the place called al-Khalṣā' (near Dhāt al-Buraq) dried up
has one sound core meaning: "pressing/pinching" and "breaking."
**al-hazīma** ("rout, defeat") in war
line of poetry attributed to Jarīr
a single core notion: scarcity of good, a shortfall of benefit
It is the opposite of acknowledgment (iqrār)
quoting al-Farazdaq's verse mentioning "the pack-beasts of a destitute man (mujḥid)."
a single regular, analogizable root whose core sense is the massing of a thing in height
الْجَبَل (al-jabal) — "the mountain,"
الْجِبِلّ (al-jibill) — a numerous multitude
a verse praising Quraysh as "the jabal of God"
identifies two unrelated base meanings for the root ج-ز-ع (j-z-ʿ)
الْجَزَعُ (al-jazaʿ, "impatience/distress") is the opposite of ṣabr (endurance)
says the root m-s-kh (مسخ) covers two separate, unrelated words
"God masakha him" = God changed his form from good/beautiful into ugly.
"You are masikh like the meat of a young weaned camel... neither sweet nor bitter."
as a sound root whose meaning he gives as selection, eminence in a thing, and elevation
al-nāṣiya, the forelock, belongs here, according to Ibn Fāris, because the hair grows from a high place
"Why do you tanṣūn your dead?" Ibn Fāris explains that she meant stretching out the dead person's forelock
the principle is removing one thing and putting another in its place
highlights.note: first view on the root's principle

highlights.text: the principle is transferring or converting one thing into another
highlights.note: second view on the root's principle

highlights.text: Copying a text — نَسْخُ الكِتَاب, transcribing a book.
a command that was formerly acted upon and is then cancelled by a new one; his example is a verse containing a command that is then abrogated by another verse
highlights.note: abrogation of one verse by another

highlights.text: something running out or being used up entirely, and thereby being cut off.
a drunk man is called nazif, because his reason (aql) has been "drained."
comparing a woman's gait to that of the nazif
a sound root with one core idea: overcoming/domination and superiority (being above)
to overcome, subdue, dominate: qahara-hu yaqharu-hu qahran
he aspired to lord it over his kinsfolk
as three separate root-meanings: (1) fear, (2) filling, (3) cutting
الرَّعْب (raʿb) is fear; the verb رَعَبْتُهُ ("I frightened him") takes the verbal noun رَعْبًا, while the noun proper is الرُّعْب (ruʿb)
one core meaning: the opposite of dryness — that is, moistness or freshness
al-raṭb and al-raṭīb — both simply mean "moist, fresh."
al-ruṭab — the well-known word for fresh, ripe dates (as opposed to dried dates)
(1) one thing overtaking or enveloping another, and (2) haste and delay
رَهِقَهُ الأمرُ = the affair overtook and covered him (equated with غَشِيَهُ)
سَلِيمُ جَنَبِ الرَّهَقَا
these three letters form one root meaning "time" (zamān).
glossing yatasannah as "it did not become like something over which the years pass and so change/spoil it"
this root has a single core meaning: **height, being raised up / elevation** (al-ʿuluww wa-l-irtifāʿ)
one core idea: joining or bringing one thing close up against another
awṣadtu al-bāb, "I awṣad-ed the door," means simply "I closed/shut it."
the finā' (courtyard or forecourt) of a dwelling
two separate words: one meaning weakness, the other denoting a time of night
وَهَنَ (wahana), imperfect yahinu, verbal noun wahn: "a thing grew weak."
The causative أَوْهَنْتُهُ (awhantuhu) means "I weakened it."
a single core idea: perceiving something together with listening/hearkening for it
to sense/perceive it and thereby listen out for it
"Mūsā sensed/conceived a fear within himself" (Ṭāhā 20:67)
he defines as pushing a thing so that it moves along, driven
yuzjī saḥāban, "He drives clouds along" (Q 24:43)
wa-ḥājatin ghayri muzjātin mina l-ḥāji, "and a need, among needs, that is not muzjāt"
